theme: David and Jonathan; Saul’s jealousy; covenant friendship
readingInstruction: Read 1 Samuel 18:1-20:42. These chapters show David’s rise, Saul’s jealousy, and the friendship of Jonathan and David. Notice how David responds to being hunted.
settingTheScene: After the victory over Goliath, David becomes a leading figure in Saul’s army. The women sing, “Saul has struck down his thousands, and David his ten thousands,” and jealousy takes root in the king’s heart. Saul tries several times to kill David. Jonathan, Saul’s son and heir, becomes David’s closest friend and risks his own father’s anger to protect him.
observation: “The soul of Jonathan was knit to the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul” (18:1).
Jonathan makes a covenant with David and gives him his robe, armor, sword, bow, and belt (18:3-4).
The women’s song makes Saul angry, and “Saul eyed David from that day on” (18:7-9).
Saul twice hurls a spear at David, and “Saul was afraid of David, because the LORD was with him” (18:11-12).
Saul offers his daughters Merab and Michal, hoping the Philistines will kill David (18:17-27).
Michal helps David escape through a window (19:11-17).
Jonathan says to David, “Whatever you say, I will do for you” (20:4), and they renew their covenant (20:16-17).
Jonathan shoots arrows as a signal, and David and Jonathan weep together as they part (20:35-42).
interpretation:
Saul’s jealousy is the central tragedy of these chapters. He had been a victorious king, and now he cannot bear to hear another man praised. The spirit that began with envy ends in murder. It illustrates how sin grows: a small resentment, left unchecked, becomes a consuming obsession. Saul even sees that the LORD is with David and that he himself has been abandoned, yet he fights against God’s chosen.

David’s behavior in the face of this is notable. He plays the harp, serves faithfully, and does not take revenge. “David behaved wisely in all his undertakings, for the LORD was with him.” He does not defend himself with a plot to take the throne. He trusts the promise that God made through Samuel.

The friendship of Jonathan and David is among the most moving in Scripture. Jonathan is the king’s heir, and David is the one who will take the throne from his house. A less godly man would have seen David as a rival. Jonathan sees him as the LORD’s anointed. He hands over his robe and his armor, a symbolic transfer of his claim to the throne. He says later that he knows David will be king (23:17). He chooses loyalty to God’s plan over personal ambition.

The covenant between the two friends is renewed in chapter 20, and the scene of their parting is full of grief. Each man is faithful to the other, and yet they must separate. Jonathan will remain with his father, and David will become a fugitive.

Faithful friendship, in this story, is a gift from God and a refuge in time of trouble. Jonathan protects David at risk to himself, and speaks the truth to his father even when it brings danger.
connection: Jesus said, “Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13). Jonathan gave up his claim to the throne for David, but Christ laid down his own life for his people. John 15:15 says, “I have called you friends.” Like David, Jesus was hated without cause (John 15:25) and hunted by those who envied him (Mark 15:10).
application:
Examine your heart for jealousy. Who do you resent because they are praised?

Give thanks for a friend who has been loyal to you, and tell them.

Ask God to make you a Jonathan, a person who puts his purposes above your own advancement.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to guard your heart against envy.
Ask him to give you Jonathan’s loyalty and David’s patience.
Thank Jesus for calling you his friend.
